title: pH-dependent stability and speciation of compound X - Stem 2

stem.value: Compound X (molar mass 250 g mol⁻¹) exists in aqueous solution as four interconverting forms, A, B, C and D. The relative amounts of the four forms depend on pH, and together they account for all of the X present in a solution.

In a stability study, 2.50 g of X was dissolved in buffer and made up to 1.00 L at each of a range of pH values. Each solution was held at 37 °C for 24 hours. During this time some X decomposed into products that are not any of forms A–D, and the extent of decomposition depended on pH.

After 24 hours, the total concentration of X remaining in each solution (all four forms combined) was measured (Figure 1). The proportion of the remaining X present as each form was also determined (Figure 2). Four pH values of particular interest are marked on both figures.

questions.prompt: Of the four marked pH values, at which is the concentration of form C highest after 24 hours, and what is that concentration?

steps.heading: Step 1 — Work out what "concentration of form C" needs
steps.body:
Start from the stem. Figure 2 shows "the proportion of the remaining X present as each form". Figure 1 shows "the total concentration of X remaining … (all four forms combined)". So Figure 2 tells you what fraction of the remaining X is C, and Figure 1 tells you how much remaining X there is. The amount of C is that fraction of that total:

$$[C]\ =\ (\text{proportion}\ \text{of}\ C)\ \times \ (\text{total}\ X\ \text{remaining})$$

This is the same idea as a class: 30% of a class of 40 is 12 students, but 55% of a class of 15 is only about 8. A bigger share of a smaller group can still be fewer people.

steps.heading: Step 2 — Read the total from Figure 1
steps.body:
Read the black curve where it crosses each dashed line (gridlines every 0.5 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹):

- pH 7: 2.0 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹ (the curve is near its trough)
- pH 10: 4.0 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹ (top of the second, smaller peak)
- pH 13: 1.5 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹
- pH 14: 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹

Notice how much smaller the pool of X is at pH 13 than at pH 10 — less than half.

steps.heading: Step 3 — Read the proportion of C from Figure 2
steps.body:
Read the pink curve (Form C) at each dashed line (gridlines every 0.05):

- pH 7: 0.10    pH 10: 0.30    pH 13: 0.55 (the pink peak)    pH 14: 0.40

steps.heading: Step 4 — Multiply and compare
steps.body:
Do the same multiplication at every marked pH, reading each total from Step 2 and each proportion from Step 3.

$$\text{pH}\ 7:\ [C]\ =\ 0.10\ \times \ 2.0\ \times \ {10}^{-3}\text{mol}\ \text{L}^{-1}$$

$$=\ 0.20\ \times \ {10}^{-3}\text{mol}\ \text{L}^{-1}$$

$$\text{pH}\ 10:\ [C]\ =\ 0.30\ \times \ 4.0\ \times \ {10}^{-3}\text{mol}\ \text{L}^{-1}$$

$$=\ 1.2\ \times \ {10}^{-3}\text{mol}\ \text{L}^{-1}$$

$$\text{pH}\ 13:\ [C]\ =\ 0.55\ \times \ 1.5\ \times \ {10}^{-3}\text{mol}\ \text{L}^{-1}$$

$$=\ 0.825\ \times \ {10}^{-3}\text{mol}\ \text{L}^{-1}$$

$$\text{pH}\ 14:\ [C]\ =\ 0.40\ \times \ 1.0\ \times \ {10}^{-3}\text{mol}\ \text{L}^{-1}$$

$$=\ 0.40\ \times \ {10}^{-3}\text{mol}\ \text{L}^{-1}$$

pH 7 loses on both counts: the pink curve is only 0.10 there, and Figure 1 is near its trough (2.0). pH 14 gives C a big share (0.40), but the pool of X is the smallest of all four (1.0). Lining the four results up — 0.20, 1.2, 0.83 and 0.40 (× 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹) — the highest [C] is at pH 10.

| **pH** | **Total X, Figure 1 (×10⁻³ mol L⁻¹)** | **Proportion of C, Figure 2 (pink)** | **[C] = proportion × total (×10⁻³ mol L⁻¹)** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 7 | 2.0 | 0.10 | 0.20 |
| **10** | **4.0** | **0.30** | **1.2** |
| 13 | 1.5 | 0.55 | 0.83 |
| 14 | 1.0 | 0.40 | 0.40 |

steps.heading: Common trap
steps.body: The question says "form C" and "highest", and the pink curve in Figure 2 has an obvious peak at pH 13 — so it feels finished. That is a reasonable instinct: in most speciation graphs the total is fixed, so the biggest share really is the biggest amount. Here it breaks, because the stem says X decomposed by different amounts at different pH, so the total is not fixed. C being 55% of a small pool (1.5) loses to C being 30% of a pool more than twice as big (4.0).

steps.heading: Mental arithmetic tip
steps.body:
- Factor out 10⁻³ first and only put it back on at the end — you are then just multiplying small decimals.
- pH 7: 0.1 × 2 = 0.2. pH 14: 0.4 × 1 = 0.4. Both are well under 1, so they drop out straight away.
- pH 10: 0.3 × 4 = 1.2. Easy.
- pH 13: round 0.55 down to 0.5 → 0.5 × 1.5 = 0.75. Even rounding 0.55 up to 0.6 gives 0.6 × 1.5 = 0.9. Either way it is under 1.2, so pH 10 wins without needing the exact value.

workedSolution.strategy: The question asks for the **concentration** of form C — an actual amount per litre. That word is the pointer. Figure 2 has the pink curve for C, but its y-axis is Proportion of total X — a share, not an amount. Figure 1 gives the amount, but for all of X, not just C. So neither figure answers on its own: you need both, combined at each marked pH, and then compare.

eliminations.reason: Multiplies 0.55 by the starting concentration (2.50 g ÷ 250 g mol⁻¹ = 1.00 × 10⁻² mol in 1.00 L), ignoring that Figure 1 shows most of X has decomposed by 24 hours — and still picks pH from Figure 2 alone.
The multiplication at pH 13 is correct, but the pH was chosen from the pink peak alone; the much smaller total at pH 13 more than cancels C's bigger share.
Reads Figure 1's total as if it were [C], forgetting that only 0.30 of the X at pH 10 is in form C.

questions.prompt: At pH 7, form B is present at a certain concentration. At pH 10, which form is present at the same concentration?

steps.heading: Step 1 — Find [B] at pH 7
steps.body:
Figure 2, green curve (Form B) at the pH 7 line: 0.30. Figure 1, black curve at pH 7: 2.0 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹.

$$[B]\ \text{at}\ \text{pH}\ 7\ =\ 0.30\ \times \ 2.0\ \times \ {10}^{-3}\text{mol}\ \text{L}^{-1}$$

$$=\ 0.60\ \times \ {10}^{-3}\text{mol}\ \text{L}^{-1}$$

This 0.60 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹ is the target to match. From here there are two paths — either is fine.

**Path A — Solve for the proportion you need**

steps.heading: Step 2A — Set up the equation
steps.body:
At pH 10, the matching form must also be at 0.60 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹. The total there is 4.0 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹ (Figure 1). Call the matching form's proportion x:

$$0.60\ \times \ {10}^{-3}=\ 4.0\ \times \ {10}^{-3}\times \ x$$

steps.heading: Step 4A — Find the curve at 0.15
steps.body:
Go to the pH 10 line in Figure 2 and look for the curve sitting at 0.15. Blue (A) is at 0.15. The others are green 0.45, pink 0.30 and yellow 0.10 — none of them is 0.15. So the form is A.

**Path B — Check every form**

steps.heading: Step 2B — Read every form at pH 10
steps.body:
Figure 1 at pH 10: 4.0 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹ — double the pH 7 total. Figure 2 at the pH 10 line:

- Blue (A): 0.15 — near the bottom of its dip
- Green (B): 0.45 — just past its peak
- Pink (C): 0.30 — on its way up
- Yellow (D): 0.10 — flat and low

steps.heading: Step 3B — Multiply each form at pH 10
Step 4B — Match to the target
steps.body:
Only form A gives 0.60 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹ at pH 10 — an exact match with [B] at pH 7. Every other form is clearly off: B (1.8) and C (1.2) are too high, D (0.40) is too low.

| **Form (pH 10)** | **Proportion, Figure 2** | **× total (4.0 × 10⁻³)** | **Concentration (×10⁻³ mol L⁻¹)** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **A** | **0.15** | **0.15 × 4.0** | **0.60 ✓** |
| B | 0.45 | 0.45 × 4.0 | 1.8 |
| C | 0.30 | 0.30 × 4.0 | 1.2 |
| D | 0.10 | 0.10 × 4.0 | 0.40 |

steps.heading: Which path?
steps.body: Both land on A. Path A is faster — one division and one read of Figure 2 — and is the one to use under exam pressure. Path B checks every form, so it doubles as its own elimination.

steps.heading: Mental arithmetic tip
steps.body: - Path A can be done without writing anything: the total doubles from pH 7 to pH 10 (2.0 → 4.0), so the matching form needs half of B's share — 0.30 ÷ 2 = 0.15.

workedSolution.strategy: The key words are **same concentration** — an amount, not a share. Just like Q1, an amount of any form is its proportion (Figure 2) multiplied by the total X remaining (Figure 1). So work out [B] at pH 7, then work out the concentration of every form at pH 10, and find the match.

eliminations.reason: Assumes the same form keeps the same concentration; B's share rises to 0.45 and the pool doubles, giving 1.8 × 10⁻³.
Matches the proportion (0.30) instead of the concentration, ignoring that the total of X doubled.
0.10 × 4.0 gives only 0.40 × 10⁻³ — lower than the target.

questions.prompt: At pH 10, what percentage of the X originally added is present as form B after 24 hours?

steps.heading: Step 1 — Starting concentration of X (stem)
steps.body:
The stem says "2.50 g of X was dissolved … and made up to 1.00 L", with a molar mass of 250 g mol⁻¹.

$$n\ =\ \frac{m}{M}$$

$$n\ =\ \frac{2.50\ g}{250\ g\ \text{mol}{}^{-1}}$$

$$n\ =\ 1.00\ \times \ {10}^{-2}\text{mol}$$

$$c\ =\ \frac{n}{V}=\ \frac{1.00\ \times \ {10}^{-2}\text{mol}}{1.00\ L}$$

$$c\ =\ 1.00\ \times \ {10}^{-2}\text{mol}\ \text{L}^{-1}$$

steps.heading: Step 2 — Read the two figures at pH 10
steps.body:
- Figure 1 (black curve): 4.0 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹ of X remains — the top of the second peak.
- Figure 2 (green curve, Form B): 0.45 — just past its peak.

steps.heading: Step 3 — Concentration of B at pH 10
steps.body:
Figure 2 says 0.45 of the remaining X is B, so multiply by the total remaining:

$$[B]\ =\ 0.45\ \times \ 4.0\ \times \ {10}^{-3}\text{mol}\ \text{L}^{-1}$$

$$[B]\ =\ 1.8\ \times \ {10}^{-3}\text{mol}\ \text{L}^{-1}$$

steps.heading: Step 4 — Compare with the starting concentration
Mental arithmetic tip
steps.body:
- Step 1 in your head: 250 goes into 2.50 exactly 0.01 times → 1.00 × 10⁻².
- Step 3: drop the decimals — 45 × 4 = 180 — then put them back → 1.8.
- Step 4: 10⁻³ ÷ 10⁻² just leaves 10⁻¹, so it's 1.8 ÷ 10 = 0.18 → 18%.

workedSolution.strategy: Two phrases do the pointing. **"Present as form B"** is an amount of B — proportion (Figure 2) × total remaining (Figure 1), as in Q1 and Q2. **"Of the X originally added"** sets the denominator: not what is left after 24 hours, but what went in at the start — and only the stem tells you that. So this question needs all three sources: the stem, Figure 1 and Figure 2.

eliminations.reason: Uses Figure 1 alone — 4.0 × 10⁻³ ÷ 1.00 × 10⁻² = 40% is the share of the original X still present in all four forms, not just B.
Uses Figure 2 alone — 45% is B's share of the remaining X, not of the X originally added.
Works out the percentage decomposed, 100% − 40% = 60%, which answers a different question.

questions.prompt: At which of the marked pH values is the concentration of form C twice that of form A?

steps.heading: Step 1 — Set up the ratio
steps.body:
Each concentration is its proportion × the total X remaining, T* (Figure 1). At the same pH, both use the same T:

$$\frac{[C]}{[A]}=\ \frac{\text{proportion}\ \text{of}\ C\ \times \ T}{\text{proportion}\ \text{of}\ A\ \times \ T}$$

$$\frac{[C]}{[A]}=\ \frac{\text{proportion}\ \text{of}\ C}{\text{proportion}\ \text{of}\ A}$$

* For reference: at pH 7, for example, T = 2.0 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹ (Figure 1), so [C] ÷ [A] = (0.10 × 2.0 × 10⁻³) ÷ (0.50 × 2.0 × 10⁻³). The 2.0 × 10⁻³ appears top and bottom and cancels — the value of T never affects the ratio.

So we need the pH values where the pink curve is exactly double the blue curve. Compare Q2: there, the two concentrations were at different pH values with different totals, so Figure 1 was essential. Here it drops out.

steps.heading: Step 2 — Read Figure 2 at every marked pH
steps.body:
Pink (C) and blue (A) at each dashed line — all values sit on the 0.05 gridlines:

- pH 7: C = 0.10, A = 0.50
- pH 10: C = 0.30, A = 0.15
- pH 13: C = 0.55, A = 0.30
- pH 14: C = 0.40, A = 0.20

steps.heading: Step 3 — Calculate the ratio at every marked pH
Common trap
steps.body: Two traps work together here. First, pH 10 comes first and checks out, so it is tempting to stop there — the "only" in options A, B and D is the warning to keep going. Second, at pH 13 form C is at its peak and A is also high, so C looks "about double" A. It is not: 0.55 is less than 2 × 0.30 = 0.60. Eyeballing is not enough when the question asks for an exact ratio.

steps.heading: Mental arithmetic tip
steps.body:
- Skip the division: double A and see if it hits C.
- pH 7: 2 × 0.50 = 1.0, not 0.10. pH 10: 2 × 0.15 = 0.30 = C ✓. pH 13: 2 × 0.30 = 0.60, not 0.55. pH 14: 2 × 0.20 = 0.40 = C ✓.

workedSolution.strategy: "Twice" is a **ratio** of two concentrations — and both are at the **same pH**. That changes things from Q1–Q3: at one pH, forms C and A share the same total of X, so the total cancels out of the ratio and only Figure 2 matters. The options also allow more than one pH, so every marked pH has to be checked — no stopping at the first hit.

eliminations.reason: Stops at the first match (pH 10) and misses pH 14, where 0.40 ÷ 0.20 is also 2.
Eyeballs pH 13 — 0.55 ÷ 0.30 ≈ 1.83, not 2 — and misses both real matches.
Finds pH 14 but skips pH 10, where 0.30 ÷ 0.15 is also 2.

questions.prompt: What mass of the dominant form at pH 7 is present in the 1.00 L solution after 24 hours? Assume all four forms have the same molar mass as X.

steps.heading: Step 1 — Identify the dominant form at pH 7
steps.body:
Figure 2 at the pH 7 line:

- Blue (A): 0.50    Green (B): 0.30    Pink (C): 0.10    Yellow (D): 0.10

Form A is dominant.

steps.heading: Step 2 — Concentration of A at pH 7
Step 3 — Moles of A in the 1.00 L solution
steps.body:
Two formulas help here. GAMSAT won't always give them, but you're expected to be familiar with them — and even if they slip your mind, following the units (mol L⁻¹ × L = mol, then mol × g mol⁻¹ = g) gets you to the same place:

- c = n / V  (concentration = moles ÷ volume)
- n = m / M  (moles = mass ÷ molar mass)

Start from c = n / V and rearrange for n by multiplying both sides by V:

$$c\ =\ \frac{n}{V}$$

$$c\ \times \ V\ =\ n$$

$$n\ =\ c\ \times \ V$$

$$n\ =\ 1.0\ \times \ {10}^{-3}\text{mol}\ \text{L}^{-1}\times \ 1.00\ L$$

$$n\ =\ 1.0\ \times \ {10}^{-3}\text{mol}$$

steps.heading: Step 4 — Mass of A
steps.body:
Start from n = m / M and rearrange for m by multiplying both sides by M:

$$n\ =\ \frac{m}{M}$$

$$n\ \times \ M\ =\ m$$

$$m\ =\ n\ \times \ M$$

$$m\ =\ 1.0\ \times \ {10}^{-3}\text{mol}\ \times \ 250\ g\ \text{mol}{}^{-1}$$

$$m\ =\ 0.25\ g$$

steps.heading: Common trap
steps.body: The stem hands you 2.50 g, and A is 0.50 of X at pH 7 — so 0.50 × 2.50 g = 1.25 g feels natural. But 2.50 g is what went in. By pH 7, Figure 1 shows only 2.0 × 10⁻³ of the original 1.00 × 10⁻² mol L⁻¹ is left — one fifth of it. The 0.50 share applies to what remains, not to what was added.

steps.heading: Mental arithmetic tip
steps.body:
- Step 4: 10⁻³ × 250 is just 250 ÷ 1000 = 0.25.
- Sanity check: all the X left at pH 7 weighs 2.0 × 10⁻³ × 250 = 0.50 g. A is half of it → 0.25 g.

workedSolution.strategy: Two jobs. First, **"dominant form"** — find which form has the biggest share at pH 7 (Figure 2). At a single pH every form shares the same total, so the biggest share is also the biggest concentration. Second, **"what mass"** — turn that form's concentration into grams: concentration → moles (n = cV) → mass (m = nM). The question tells you to use X's molar mass (250 g mol⁻¹) for every form.

eliminations.reason: Divides instead of multiplies — 1.0 × 10⁻³ ÷ 250 = 4.0 × 10⁻⁶ — which does not even come out in grams.
Uses Figure 1's total alone — 2.0 × 10⁻³ × 250 = 0.50 g is the mass of all four forms, not just A.
Applies the proportion to the original mass — 0.50 × 2.50 g = 1.25 g — ignoring that most of X has decomposed.
